lessons.title: Reading 10-Year ROCE and ROE Trends on Screener.in

body.text: One year of ROCE is a snapshot. Ten years is a story. The moat is in the shape of the line, not in any single number.

children.text: Chapter 1 showed that ROCE above the cost of capital is the financial fingerprint of a moat. This lesson turns that idea into a repeatable routine on Screener.in: where to find the data, the five patterns a 10-year ROCE history can take, the simple statistics that expose each one, and the adjustments that stop the headline number from misleading you.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Search any NSE or BSE listed company. Scroll to the Ratios section for the year-by-year ROCE % history.

children.text: Five Patterns a 10-Year ROCE History Can Take

cells: 1. Steady and high
Stays well above 15% every year, with a shallow dip in bad years
A likely moat; now identify its source
2. Cyclical
Swings from single digits to very high and back
A commodity or cyclical business; judge on the full-cycle average and the troughs
3. High but declining
Starts very high and slides steadily year after year
A moat that may be eroding; find out why
4. Low but improving
Rises steadily from below the hurdle to above it
A moat possibly being built, or a turnaround; needs a business reason
5. Steady and low
Stays near or below 15% every year
No moat, whatever the story says

children.text: Four Numbers That Summarise the Decade
Eyeballing a chart is useful, but a few simple statistics make comparisons across companies fast and honest.
Median ROCE:
the middle value of the ten years. It is less distorted by one exceptional year than the average.
Minimum ROCE:
the worst year. A moat business keeps even its worst year respectable.
Years above the hurdle:
how many of the ten years cleared a 15% pre-tax ROCE.
Latest three-year average vs decade median:
whether returns are currently above or below the company's own long-run norm.

children.text: Look at Company Y. Its average of 19.0% sits comfortably above the 15% hurdle and looks respectable. But its minimum of 6% and only 5 years above the hurdle reveal a cyclical business. Company Z has cleared the hurdle every year, yet its last three years average 19.0%, well below its decade median of 27.5%, and the trend is heading straight for the hurdle. Company X is the only one that is high, steady, and not declining.

body.title: Why median and minimum beat the average

children.text: An average adds up every year and divides by ten, so one spectacular year can lift it a lot. Company Y's FY23 figure of 38% pulls its average up even though most of its years were below 20%.

The median simply takes the middle of the sorted values, so a single outlier barely moves it. The minimum tells you what happens when conditions turn against the business, which is exactly when a moat proves itself.

A practical rule: a company whose median is comfortably above 20% and whose minimum stays above 15% has a strong claim to a moat fingerprint. Then you still need a business reason from Chapters 2 to 4.

body.title: Read the Decade
body.question: A company's ROCE over ten years reads: 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 17, 21, 23, 25, 26. What is the best interpretation?
options: A cyclical business at its peak
A business whose returns are steadily improving, possibly building an advantage, which needs a clear business reason before calling it a moat
body.explanation: This is the "low but improving" pattern: a steady climb with only one small dip, from below the hurdle to well above it. It is not cyclical (no sharp swings) and not yet established (only the last several years are strong). It could reflect a moat being built, such as growing scale or brand, or an operational turnaround. Look for the business reason.

children.text: ROE and ROCE Side by Side
Checking ROE next to ROCE reveals how the company is financed and whether the headline return is flattered.

body.caption: Reading the gap between ROE and ROCE

cells: ROE far above ROCE
Debt is magnifying returns to shareholders
Borrowings trend and interest coverage; is the business as good as ROE suggests?
ROE close to or slightly below ROCE
Normal for a low-debt company, since ROE is after tax and ROCE on Screener.in is before tax
Nothing unusual; this is typical for a conservatively financed business
ROE rising while ROCE is flat
Buybacks, large dividends, or new debt are shrinking equity
Changes in reserves and borrowings in the balance sheet
Both low but cash is huge
Idle cash is dragging down both ratios
Calculate core ROCE excluding cash, below

body.text: Screener.in shows ROCE, not ROE, as the main return ratio for most non-financial companies because it is harder to flatter with debt. For banks and NBFCs the logic flips: borrowing is their raw material, so use ROE and return on assets instead. A 10-year ROCE trend on a bank tells you very little.

children.text: Adjust for Cash: Core ROCE

markDefs.definition: Return on the capital actually used in operations: EBIT excluding other income, divided by capital employed excluding cash and investments. It shows the true return of the operating business.

children.text: Cash-rich companies, common among Indian IT services and some consumer firms, can show a lower ROCE than their operating business deserves. Idle cash sits in capital employed, and the interest it earns sits in other income. Strip both out to get
core ROCE

Example: EBIT is ₹1,000 crore, including ₹150 crore of other income. Capital employed is ₹5,000 crore, including ₹2,000 crore of cash and investments. Reported ROCE is ₹1,000 crore ÷ ₹5,000 crore = 20%. Core ROCE is ₹850 crore ÷ ₹3,000 crore = 28.3%. The operating business earns far more than the headline suggests.

body.title: Calculate Core ROCE
body.prompt: A company reports EBIT of ₹600 crore, which includes ₹100 crore of other income. Capital employed is ₹3,500 crore, including ₹1,500 crore of cash and liquid investments. What is its core ROCE?
body.explanation: Core EBIT = ₹600 crore − ₹100 crore = ₹500 crore. Core capital employed = ₹3,500 crore − ₹1,500 crore = ₹2,000 crore. Core ROCE = ₹500 crore ÷ ₹2,000 crore = 25%, compared with a reported ROCE of about 17.1%.

children.text: Screen for Moat Fingerprints Across the Market

Screener.in lets you run a custom query across all listed companies. The exact ratio names are available in the query builder's suggestions as you type; a moat-oriented screen typically combines long-run ROCE, current ROCE, and low leverage.

body.code:
Average return on capital employed 10Years > 20 AND
Return on capital employed > 18 AND
Debt to equity < 0.5 AND
Market Capitalization > 1000
body.caption: Example Screener.in query syntax (not actual SQL). Confirm ratio names in the query builder before running.

children.text: A screen is a starting list, not a buy list. Every company it returns still needs the pattern check, the core ROCE adjustment where cash is large, and a business reason for the returns.

body.title: Complete the Rule
body.textWithBlank: When comparing ROCE histories, the ___ ROCE across ten years tells you how the business performs when conditions turn against it.
body.explanation: The worst year shows how much protection the business has in a downturn. Moat businesses keep even their minimum ROCE respectable.

body.title: The Screener Shortlist
body.scenario: Your ROCE screen returns a mid cap chemicals company with a 10-year average ROCE of 24%. Looking closer, its ROCE was 12% to 16% from FY16 to FY20, jumped to 38% in FY22 and 41% in FY23 during a period of supply disruptions from China, and has since fallen back to 19% in FY25. Its ROE was higher than ROCE in the peak years, and borrowings have risen to fund a new plant.
body.prompt: Does this company have a moat fingerprint? Walk through the pattern and statistics you would check.
body.modelAnswer: The average of 24% is flattered by two exceptional years linked to a temporary supply disruption. The pattern looks cyclical or event-driven rather than steady: five years of 12% to 16%, around or below the hurdle, a spike, and a reversion. The median is likely much lower than 24%, and the minimum is around 12%. The last three years show a sharp decline from the peak. ROE above ROCE, with borrowings rising, shows leverage is now magnifying shareholder returns. The new plant will also add capital work-in-progress, depressing ROCE temporarily. Before calling this a moat, you would want to see ROCE settling comfortably above 20% once conditions normalise, a specific business reason such as a patented process, switching costs with customers, or cost leadership, and evidence that the plant earns similar returns once running. On current evidence, this is a cyclical beneficiary, not a proven moat.

body.label: The moat fingerprint, as a rule of thumb
body.value: Median ROCE above 20%, minimum above 15%, no steady downtrend
body.context: Pre-tax ROCE from Screener.in, adjusted for large cash balances. Then find the business reason.

body.title: Build a 10-Year ROCE Profile
steps: Pick three listed non-financial companies in the same industry
Check the consolidated view on Screener.in and copy ten years of ROCE % from the Ratios section into a spreadsheet
Calculate the median, minimum, years above 15%, and last three-year average for each
Classify each company into one of the five patterns
For any company with large cash balances, calculate core ROCE for the latest year
Compare ROE with ROCE and note any company where debt explains most of the gap

body.text: Companies W, X, Y, and Z and the chemicals scenario are hypothetical. Screener.in section layouts and ratio names may change; confirm them on the site. Nothing here is an investment recommendation.

points: A moat shows up in the shape of a 10-year ROCE history, not in a single year's figure
Five common patterns are steady and high, cyclical, high but declining, low but improving, and steady and low
Use median, minimum, years above a 15% pre-tax hurdle, and the last three-year average to compare companies honestly
Compare ROE with ROCE: a large gap usually means debt is magnifying returns
Core ROCE, excluding other income and idle cash, shows the real return of cash-rich businesses
Screener.in screens produce a starting list; each result still needs pattern analysis and a business reason
